name: Oats / rice-and-chicken carbs for bulking

lead: A standard bulk built on oats, rice and chicken means eating above maintenance calories with inexpensive carbohydrate and lean-protein staples to add muscle and build a bigger physique.

The chain is a calorie surplus supplying fuel for hard training, with adequate protein supporting muscle growth alongside resistance training. Wikipedia reports a well-established link between positive energy balance and muscle growth; the specific foods have not been trialled as a set.

paras: Lifters eat large portions of oats at breakfast and rice with chicken at other meals, raising portions to stay in surplus, and favour slower-digesting carbohydrates. Bulks typically run for months, with muscle added gradually.
Larger surpluses and longer bulks add more body fat, and some lifters report needing a harder cut afterward.

angle.text: Lifters build a bulk around oats, rice and chicken to eat in a calorie surplus affordably and add muscle for a bigger physique. Cheap carbs supply fuel for hard training, and a surplus with enough protein supports growth. The link between positive energy balance and muscle gain is well established.

lead: A "standard bulk" built around oats, rice and chicken refers to eating in a calorie surplus using inexpensive carbohydrate and lean-protein staples in order to gain muscle. Bulking in general means eating above maintenance energy needs, and Wikipedia reports a well-established link between positive energy balance and muscle growth.[1]

Bodybuilding references describe preferences for slower-digesting carbohydrates, and note that a larger surplus or longer bulk adds more body fat.[1] The specific foods oats, rice and chicken are not singled out in the sources reviewed.

paras: Bodybuilders commonly alternate an off-season bulking phase with a pre-contest cut of roughly 12 to 14 weeks.[1] Clean bulking aims for muscle with limited fat gain, and dirty bulking uses a large surplus with less tracking; the latter tends to add more fat.[1]

Protein recommendations vary among experts, with some favouring about 1 g per pound of body weight and others more or less.[1] Controlled studies using calorimetry found no metabolic advantage of eating five to seven meals over three.[1]
No studies found on oats, rice and chicken as a specific bulking diet.
